title: On Not Shooting Sitting Birds
description: A short story by Jean Rhys, collected in Sleep It Off Lady (1976), her last collection, after an earlier printing in The New Yorker: a young West Indian woman in London recalls an evening with an Englishman that goes wrong over a story about shooting birds.
plot_or_argument: The narrator, a young woman from the West Indies living in London, goes out with an Englishman she wants to please. Trying to interest him, she talks about her island and about going out shooting there; when he gathers that she has shot sitting birds, the one thing his sporting code forbids, he is put off, the evening falls flat and he drops her for good.
narrative_structure: A brief first-person reminiscence, one of the stories of Sleep It Off Lady that follow a Caribbean heroine from girlhood through Edwardian London.
meter_and_prosody: Spare, understated prose and dialogue in which the comedy of manners is barely distinguished from humiliation.
historical_context: Sleep It Off Lady, published by André Deutsch in October 1976, arranges sixteen stories chronologically from the Dominica of the 1890s to the old age of its last heroines; Rhys died in 1979.
literary_significance: One of the late stories that confirmed Rhys's revival after Wide Sargasso Sea; Norton pairs it with "The Day They Burned the Books".
bibliographical_notes: Collected in Sleep It Off Lady (London: André Deutsch, 1976), which lists it among its sixteen stories; earlier printed in The New Yorker (date not established). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 570.
thematic_analysis: Misunderstanding across nationality and class, the outsider's failed attempt to speak the codes of English respectability, and the woman's vulnerability and self-possession in an affair that does not happen.
summary: An evening out between a young woman from the Caribbean and an Englishman she hopes to impress, and the remark about shooting birds at home that ends his interest in her.
research_notes: Wikipedia's summary of the collection calls the heroine Elsa; whether she is named in this story was not checked. The date of the New Yorker printing was not established, so 1976 is the date recorded.

title: Waiting for Godot
description: Samuel Beckett's tragicomedy in two acts, in which two tramps, Vladimir and Estragon, wait by a leafless tree on a country road for a Mr Godot, who never comes. Beckett wrote it in French between October 1948 and January 1949; En attendant Godot was published in 1952 and first performed in Paris in January 1953, and his own English version, recorded here because it is the text Norton prints, was published in 1954 and first staged in London in 1955. It is his best-known work and one of the most influential plays of the century.
plot_or_argument:
Act I. On a country road by a bare tree, in the evening, Estragon struggles to pull off his boot and tells Vladimir that he spent the night in a ditch and was beaten. They talk at length, about the two thieves crucified with Christ and why only one gospel says one was saved, about hanging themselves from the tree, and about the man they are waiting for, Godot, though they are not sure they have ever met him, whether this is the right place or the right day, or what they asked him for. Pozzo arrives, driving Lucky before him on a rope and laden with his bags. Pozzo eats chicken while Estragon begs for the bones, lectures on the twilight, and says he is taking Lucky to the fair to sell him. At Pozzo's order Lucky dances and then, told to think, pours out a torrent of broken academic and theological speech about a personal God and a shrinking, petrifying humanity, which ends only when the others seize his hat. Pozzo and Lucky leave. A boy comes with a message from Mr Godot: he will not come this evening but surely tomorrow. The boy minds the goats; his brother, who minds the sheep, is beaten. Night falls and the moon rises. 'Well, shall we go?' 'Yes, let's go.' They do not move.

Act II. The next day, the same time and place; the tree has a few leaves. Vladimir sings a circular song about a dog; Estragon has been beaten again and remembers little of yesterday. To pass the time they abuse each other, make up, exercise, play at being Pozzo and Lucky and juggle hats, including the one Lucky left behind. Pozzo and Lucky return: Pozzo is now blind and Lucky dumb, and they fall in a heap from which Vladimir and Estragon, after much delay, raise them. Pozzo remembers nothing of the day before and, asked when his blindness came, rages that one day is like any other: they give birth astride of a grave, the light gleams an instant, then it is night once more. When they have gone Vladimir, watching Estragon sleep, wonders whether he too is asleep and what he will remember of today. The boy returns, or another like him, says he did not come yesterday and repeats the message: Mr Godot will not come this evening but tomorrow. Godot, the boy says, does nothing, and his beard is white. The two try to hang themselves with the cord that holds up Estragon's trousers, which breaks, and the trousers fall. They will hang themselves tomorrow, unless Godot comes; then they will be saved. 'Well? Shall we go?' 'Yes, let's go.' They do not move.
narrative_structure: Two acts of nearly identical design, the second a variation of the first with the decline of Pozzo and Lucky; a single setting (a country road, a tree, evening); cross-talk, repetition, routines, pauses and silences; Lucky's monologue as the one unbroken torrent of speech; each act ends with an exchange contradicted by the stage direction 'They do not move'.
principal_characters: Vladimir (Didi); Estragon (Gogo); Pozzo; Lucky; a Boy
literary_form: Play (tragicomedy in two acts; the author's English version of En attendant Godot)
meter_and_prosody: Spare, rhythmic dialogue built from short exchanges, repetitions and echoes; the comedy of the music hall, the circus and silent film (hats, boots, falling trousers) set against lyrical and philosophical passages; an English version that keeps the French text's plainness while adding its own idiom.
historical_context: Beckett, an Irish writer living in Paris, turned to writing in French after the Second World War, in which he had served in the Resistance; he wrote the play between his novels Malone meurt and L'Innommable. Roger Blin directed the premiere at the Théâtre de Babylone in January 1953. Martin Esslin later placed it at the head of what he called the Theatre of the Absurd.
literary_significance: Voted the most significant English-language play of the twentieth century in a 1998 poll by the Royal National Theatre, the play transformed modern drama in Britain, Ireland, Europe and America, freeing the stage from plot and psychological realism and influencing Pinter, Stoppard and generations of dramatists. It made Beckett famous and was central to the case for his Nobel Prize in Literature (1969). It is constantly revived, adapted and studied, and Norton prints it entire.
bibliographical_notes: Written in French between 9 October 1948 and 29 January 1949; published as En attendant Godot (Paris, 1952) and first performed at the Théâtre de Babylone, Paris, on 5 January 1953. Beckett's own English version was published in 1954 and first performed in London in 1955. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 613.
thematic_analysis: Waiting is the play's subject and its form: in the absence of Godot, whom the characters and audiences have read as God, meaning, rescue or nothing at all, life becomes a matter of filling time with talk, routine and play. The pairing of Vladimir and Estragon, mutually dependent and unable to part, and of Pozzo and Lucky, master and slave bound by a rope, gives the play its account of human relations, of habit, cruelty and need. Memory fails, time repeats with small changes, and suffering is unexplained; the story of the two thieves frames the question of arbitrary salvation. Yet the play is also a comedy of friendship and endurance, in which the companions keep each other going and the music-hall routines are a kind of courage.
summary: Two acts on two successive evenings, each with the same shape: Vladimir and Estragon pass the time waiting for Godot; the master Pozzo and his servant Lucky pass by; a boy brings word that Godot will not come today but surely tomorrow; the two decide to go and do not move. Between the acts Pozzo has gone blind and Lucky dumb, and the tree has put out a few leaves.
critical_context: Critics have called it one of the most enigmatic plays of modern literature, and its readings are religious, philosophical, classical, social, psychoanalytical and biographical. Esslin's The Theatre of the Absurd (1961) made it the type of a theatre that presents the absurdity of the human condition without arguing about it; Beckett himself refused to explain Godot. Its first English-language reception was divided, until critics such as Harold Hobson and Kenneth Tynan championed it.
research_notes: The composition dates, the French publication and premiere, the London premiere year and the 1998 poll come from Wikipedia (citing Federman and Fletcher's bibliography and Ackerley and Gontarski). The English publication (Grove Press, New York, 1954), the London director (Peter Hall, Arts Theatre) and the reviewers Hobson and Tynan are general knowledge, not checked against a consulted source; so are Beckett's war service, the place of the play among his French novels, Esslin's date, the Nobel year and the play's influence on later dramatists.

title: In Praise of Limestone
description: A poem by W. H. Auden, written on Ischia in May 1948, the first he wrote in Italy, and published in Horizon in July 1948 before its collection in Nones (1951). A meditation on the Mediterranean limestone landscape as the one human landscape, it is regarded as central to his canon and one of his finest poems.
plot_or_argument: If there is one landscape that 'we, the inconstant ones' are consistently homesick for, the poem begins, it is because limestone dissolves in water: its rounded hills, caves, springs and short distances shape a people who are local, sensual, quarrelsome and unable to imagine a god of rage. The best and worst never stayed there long but sought immoderate soils: granite wastes for the saints-to-be, clays and gravels for the would-be tyrants, who left slamming the door, and the oceanic whisper for the really reckless: 'I am the solitude that asks and promises nothing'. The speaker admits that the landscape seems historically unimportant, and that the poet, admired for calling the sun the sun, is made uneasy by it. Yet it makes a further point: in a world where sins can be forgiven and bodies rise from the dead, the blessed will not care from what angle they are seen, having nothing to hide. Dear, he ends, I know nothing of either, but when I try to imagine a faultless love or the life to come, what I hear is the murmur of underground streams, what I see is a limestone landscape.
narrative_structure: A single long verse paragraph moving from description through the catalogue of other soils and the poet's unease to the theological turn and the closing confession.
literary_form: Poem (meditative and topographical, in long and short unrhymed lines)
meter_and_prosody: Conversational, discursive and witty, with long sentences and a relaxed, unrhymed line; a mixture of plain speech and theological vocabulary.
historical_context: Auden, who had moved to the United States in 1939 and returned to Christianity, spent the spring and summer of 1948 on Ischia with Chester Kallman; the poem opens the Italian phase of his work. He revised it from 1958 and gave it a prominent place in Collected Shorter Poems, 1922-1957 (1966).
literary_significance: Called sui generis and even the first postmodern pastoral, it is one of the most studied of Auden's later poems and a central text for his post-war turn to the body, the ordinary and Christian belief.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Horizon (July 1948); collected in Nones (1951); revised version from 1958. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 683.
thematic_analysis: The landscape is read as an allegory of Mediterranean civilisation, set against the Protestant, rationalist 'Gothic North', and, by Edward Mendelson and others, as an allegory of the human body, at the human scale and indifferent to great events. The poem rejects abstraction and the will to be little gods, and justifies the ordinary and the bodily in theological terms, with an erotic warmth addressed to 'Dear'.
summary: A description of a limestone landscape and of the people it forms, set against the granite, clay and ocean that tempt saints, tyrants and romantic solitaries, and ending in a vision of faultless love and the life to come as a limestone landscape.
critical_context: Anthony Hecht wrote a whole essay on it (1979); Rebecca Price Parkin, Alan W. France, Rainer Emig and Hugh Underhill have read it variously as a facsimile of immediacy, as a contrast of Mediterranean South and Gothic North, and as an erotics of the ground.
research_notes: The poem's metre (Auden wrote it in syllabic lines) is general knowledge, not checked against a consulted source; the form field therefore describes the lines only as long and short. Which version Norton prints was not checked.

title: The Shield of Achilles
description: A poem by W. H. Auden, first published in 1952 and the title poem of his collection The Shield of Achilles (1955), which won the National Book Award for Poetry in 1956. It rewrites Homer's description of the shield of Achilles in the Iliad: Thetis looks for scenes of peace and plenty and finds the barren, impersonal violence of the modern world.
plot_or_argument: Thetis looks over Hephaestus's shoulder for vines and olive trees, marble cities and ships on untamed seas, but on the shining metal he has put an artificial wilderness under a sky like lead. An unintelligible multitude, a million eyes and boots in line, waits on a featureless plain while a voice without a face proves by statistics that some cause was just; they march away enduring a belief whose logic brings them somewhere else to grief. She looks for ritual pieties, white flower-garlanded heifers and libation, and sees instead a barbed-wire enclosure where bored officials lounge and sentries sweat, while a crowd of ordinary decent folk watch three pale figures led forth and bound to posts, unable to hope for help. She looks for athletes at their games and dancers moving to music, and sees a weed-choked field where a ragged urchin, aimless and alone, throws a stone at a bird; he takes for granted that girls are raped and that two boys knife a third, and has never heard of any world where promises are kept or one could weep because another wept. The thin-lipped armourer limps away, and Thetis cries out in dismay at what the god has made to please her son, the strong, iron-hearted, man-slaying Achilles, who would not live long.
narrative_structure: Short-lined eight-line stanzas, giving what Thetis looks for, alternate with seven-line stanzas of longer lines in rhyme royal (ababbcc), describing what Hephaestus makes; a final short-lined stanza gives Thetis's cry.
literary_form: Poem (two alternating stanza forms, one in rhyme royal)
meter_and_prosody: The lyric, ballad-like short stanzas contrast with the grave, documentary long stanzas; flat, abstract diction for the modern scenes, sensuous imagery for the Homeric ones.
historical_context: Written in the aftermath of the Second World War, the camps and the show trials, and published in the first years of the Cold War; the 1955 collection gathers poems of about 1951-1954, including the sequences Bucolics and Horae Canonicae.
literary_significance: One of Auden's best-known poems and a classic modern ekphrasis, widely anthologised as a poem about war and atrocity; the collection it names won the National Book Award.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1952 (the periodical was not identified in the sources consulted); the title poem of The Shield of Achilles (London: Faber and Faber, 1955). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 685.
thematic_analysis: Against Homer's world, where even in war the imagination ran to scenes of peace, Auden sets a modern world of mass obedience, statistics and bureaucratic killing, of spectators who do nothing and of children for whom violence is normal. The execution of the three figures recalls the Crucifixion; the poem is an indictment of the totalitarian age and of the banality of violence.
summary: Thetis watches Hephaestus making the shield for her son; the scenes she expects and the scenes he makes: a faceless army, an execution watched by a passive crowd, a ragged urchin in a vacant field; her dismay.
research_notes: Wikipedia cites John Fuller's commentary and Mendelson's Later Auden in general and Rick Brown's essay on the banality of violence; none was consulted. The Crucifixion reading is a common one, stated here from the text.

title: The Children of the Poor
description: A sequence of sonnets by Gwendolyn Brooks that opens 'The Womanhood', the final part of Annie Allen (1949), the book that made her the first African American to win the Pulitzer Prize. A mother asks what she can give her children, who are poor and black, to carry them through the world.
plot_or_argument: The sonnets speak as a mother. In the best-known, she asks what she can give her children, who are poor, 'adjudged the leastwise of the land', her 'sweetest lepers', who demand no luxuries but have begged her for a firm shape, crying that they are unfinished, made by a hand less than sure. Her hand is full of mode, design and device, but she lacks access to her proper stone, and no plan, grief or love will be enough to ratify her little halves as they cross an autumn freezing everywhere. Other sonnets ask whether she should teach them to pray, and urge that they first fight, then fiddle.
narrative_structure: Petrarchan and Shakespearean sonnets, compressed and syntactically intricate, in the sequence that begins the volume's final part.
literary_form: Sonnet sequence (in 'The Womanhood', the last part of Annie Allen)
meter_and_prosody: Dense, Latinate diction and inversions ('My hand is stuffed with mode, design, device') set against plain speech; the formal sonnet bent to a mother's anger and tenderness.
historical_context: Annie Allen, published by Harper and Brothers on 1 October 1949, follows its heroine from girlhood through the mock epic 'The Anniad' to 'The Womanhood', where she looks at a world she would like to change; it won Poetry's Eunice Tietjens Prize and the 1950 Pulitzer Prize.
literary_significance: The sonnets are among Brooks's most admired formal achievements and a key text of mid-century African American poetry; Norton prints the sequence, or part of it, as its representation of Annie Allen.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Annie Allen (New York: Harper and Brothers, 1949), in 'The Womanhood'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, vol. E (the Norton list gives 'The Womanhood: The Children of the Poor (II)'; no page numbers).
thematic_analysis: The limits of a mother's power against poverty and racism, and the place of art, faith and resistance in raising children who are 'contraband' in their own country.
summary: A mother's meditation, in sonnets, on what she can give her poor children, on whether to teach them to pray, and on what they must do to survive.
research_notes: The quotations and the content of the sonnets are stated from the text, not from a consulted source, and the number of sonnets Norton prints was not established. Recorded under 'The Children of the Poor', the sequence's title.

title: We Real Cool
description: A poem by Gwendolyn Brooks, written in 1959 and published in her third collection, The Bean Eaters (1960). In eight short lines, seven young pool players boast of the life they lead and arrive at its end, 'We / Die soon.' It is one of the most famous and most taught American poems of the century.
plot_or_argument: The poem is spoken by seven pool players at a hall called the Golden Shovel. 'We real cool,' they begin, and in short boasts they say what they do: they left school, they lurk late, they strike straight, they sing sin and thin gin, they jazz June. Each line ends on 'We', so that every boast is carried over into the next line, until the last, which has no 'We' after it: 'We / Die soon.' The swagger collapses into the knowledge, or the fate, the boasting has concealed.
narrative_structure: Four couplets of three-word lines (after the two-line heading), with internal and end rhyme and the pronoun 'We' placed at the end of each line but the last, so that the enjambment enacts the players' hesitation.
meter_and_prosody: Monosyllabic, vernacular speech with the syncopation of jazz; alliteration ('strike straight', 'sing sin') and the dropped copula of Black English.
historical_context: Brooks said the poem came from passing a pool hall full of boys in her Chicago neighbourhood and wondering how they felt about themselves. The Bean Eaters (1960) takes many of its subjects from the news of the civil rights years.
literary_significance: Cited as one of the most celebrated examples of jazz poetry, it has been printed on broadsides, reprinted in textbooks, banned in places for 'jazz', and answered by later writers; Terrance Hayes's 'golden shovel' form takes its name from it.
bibliographical_notes: Written in 1959; published in The Bean Eaters (New York: Harper, 1960), Brooks's third collection. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, vol. E (no page numbers).
thematic_analysis: Youth, rebellion and doom: the players defy school and the establishment, which Brooks said June represents, but their cool is fragile. Brooks said the 'we's should be spoken softly, as if the boys were questioning the validity of their existence; the poem is compassionate rather than censorious.
summary: Under the heading 'The Pool Players. / Seven at the Golden Shovel', the players list what they do: leave school, lurk late, strike straight, sing sin, thin gin, jazz June, and die soon.
research_notes: Brooks's comments come from her 1970 interview with George Stavros in Contemporary Literature and a recorded reading, as reported by Wikipedia; neither was consulted directly. The publisher's name is general knowledge.

title: The Bean Eaters
description: The title poem of Gwendolyn Brooks's third collection, The Bean Eaters (1960): an old couple eat their dinner of beans in a rented back room crowded with the keepsakes of their life.
plot_or_argument: 'They eat beans mostly, this old yellow pair.' Dinner is a casual affair of plain chipware, creaking wood and tin flatware. They are two who are 'Mostly Good', two who have lived their day but keep on putting on their clothes and putting things away, and remembering, with twinklings and twinges, as they lean over the beans in their rented back room full of beads and receipts and dolls and cloths, tobacco crumbs, vases and fringes.
narrative_structure: Three brief stanzas of irregular line length and loose rhyme, ending in a long catalogue line.
meter_and_prosody: Plain description with ironic touches ('Dinner is a casual affair') and the closing list of objects, which holds the couple's past.
historical_context: The Bean Eaters (1960) is the collection in which Brooks turned increasingly to the lives of poor Chicagoans and to the public events of the civil rights years.
literary_significance: One of Brooks's most anthologised short poems; Gale's Poetry for Students gives it an entry of its own.
bibliographical_notes: The title poem of The Bean Eaters (New York: Harper, 1960). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, vol. E (no page numbers).
thematic_analysis: Poverty and old age, the dignity of routine, and memory, presented with sympathy and without sentiment; critics have read the couple's colour and circumstances as a comment on race and class.
summary: An elderly couple at a plain meal; their routine of dressing and tidying; their memories, stirred by the objects that fill their room.
research_notes: Text and readings from Gale's Poetry for Students entry, which cites Norris B. Clark's essay in A Life Distilled (1987) for a reading of the poem as primarily about race.

title: A Bronzeville Mother Loiters in Mississippi. Meanwhile, a Mississippi Mother Burns Bacon
alternative_titles: A Bronzeville Mother Loiters in Mississippi
description: A long poem by Gwendolyn Brooks on the murder of Emmett Till, published in The Bean Eaters (1960). It is told through the consciousness of a white woman modelled on Carolyn Bryant, whose husband was one of the men accused of killing the fourteen-year-old Chicago boy in Mississippi in 1955, as she makes breakfast in her kitchen after the acquittal.
plot_or_argument: From childhood the woman has imagined life as a ballad, with herself as the milk-white maid, a Dark Villain and a Fine Prince who rescues her. Now, in her kitchen, burning the bacon as she makes breakfast after the trial, she finds the story will not fit: the villain was a child of fourteen, his eyes and his mother's grief haunt her, and the prince is her husband, who has killed and been acquitted. When he slaps one of their small children across the face, the blood she has been imagining seems to rise in the room, and as he embraces her she can think only of the killing. She does not scream, but a hatred for him bursts into glorious flower, bigger than all magnolias. The poem ends by pointing to the last bleak news of the ballad: 'The last quatrain.'
narrative_structure: Long free-verse paragraphs of varying line length following the woman's thoughts through a single morning, with the ballad as a frame she keeps testing; the title's full stop divides it into two headline-like sentences, and the last line hands over to 'The Last Quatrain of the Ballad of Emmett Till'.
literary_form: Poem (long narrative and dramatic poem in free verse)
meter_and_prosody: Interior monologue in the third person, mixing fairy-tale and ballad diction with domestic realism and newspaper fact; recurrent imagery of red, blood and magnolias.
historical_context: Emmett Till, a black Chicago teenager visiting relatives, was murdered in August 1955 after being accused of whistling at Carolyn Bryant; his mother's open-casket funeral and the acquittal of the killers made the case a catalyst of the civil rights movement. Brooks, a mother in Chicago, published the poem five years later.
literary_significance: Brooks's most ambitious poem in The Bean Eaters and one of the major literary responses to the Till case, unusual in imagining it through the white wife.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Bean Eaters (New York: Harper, 1960). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, vol. E (no page numbers).
thematic_analysis: The poem exposes the racial and sexual myths, the ballad of white womanhood threatened and avenged, that justified lynching, and shows the white wife's complicity breaking under the recognition of what was done in her name. Setting the poem in a kitchen makes racialised violence part of everyday domestic life; images of red and seeping blood bind it to its companion poem about Till's mother.
summary: The young wife's reflections on the ballad she had imagined herself in, on the 'Dark Villain' who turned out to be a child, on her husband and her own children, and on the boy's mother; her growing revulsion from her husband.
critical_context: A scholarly article on Brooks's poetic response to the lynching reads the pair of poems as a study of Carolyn Bryant's consciousness and of Mamie Bradley's grief, both set in the kitchen and joined by images of blood; encyclopedias of motherhood and the National Portrait Gallery present them as Brooks's moving meditations on the aftermath of the murder.
research_notes: The plot is stated from the text; the reading of the woman as Carolyn Bryant comes from the ResearchGate abstract and the SAGE encyclopedia entry. The facts of the Till case are general knowledge.

title: The Last Quatrain of the Ballad of Emmett Till
description: A short poem by Gwendolyn Brooks that follows 'A Bronzeville Mother Loiters in Mississippi' in The Bean Eaters (1960) and completes its ballad: Emmett Till's mother, after the murder and the burial, alone in a red room.
plot_or_argument: Subtitled 'after the murder, after the burial', the poem shows Emmett's mother, a pretty-faced woman the tint of pulled taffy, sitting in a red room drinking black coffee. She kisses her killed boy, and she is sorry. The poem closes on chaos in windy grays through a red prairie.
narrative_structure: A handful of very short lines, presented as the 'last quatrain' that the preceding poem announces.
meter_and_prosody: Understated, almost flat statement ('And she is sorry') and a closing image of colour and weather.
historical_context: Mamie Till Bradley's insistence on an open casket made her son's murder in 1955 a national cause; Brooks, writing from Chicago, gives her the last word of the pair of poems.
literary_significance: Paired with 'A Bronzeville Mother' as Brooks's response to the Till case, it is among her most frequently anthologised short poems.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Bean Eaters (New York: Harper, 1960). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, vol. E (no page numbers).
thematic_analysis: Grief reduced to its barest gestures, and the private mourning that answers the public ballad of the companion poem; red binds the room, the prairie and the blood of the murder.
summary: Till's mother in Chicago after her son's funeral: her appearance, her red room, her black coffee, her kiss for her killed boy, and the chaos of the landscape.
research_notes: The quoted phrases are stated from the text.

title: The Blackstone Rangers
description: A poem in three parts by Gwendolyn Brooks on the Blackstone Rangers, a Chicago street gang, published in In the Mecca (1968), the book of her turn towards the Black Arts Movement.
plot_or_argument: In 'As Seen by Disciplines' the Rangers are thirty at the corner, black, raw, ready, sores in the city that do not want to heal. 'The Leaders' names Jeff, Gene, Geronimo and Bop, who are hardly the dupes of downtown, hardly Belafonte, King or Malcolm X, and whose country is a nation on no map. 'Gang Girls' follows Mary Ann, a rose in a whiskey glass, whose year passes in the narrow world of the gang, save for her love.
narrative_structure: Three titled sections of different length and manner, moving from the outside view to the leaders and then to a single girl.
meter_and_prosody: Compressed, inventive diction and wordplay ('They cancel, cure and curry'), mixing street names and lyrical figures; freer forms than her earlier work.
historical_context: In the Mecca (Harper and Row, 1968), Brooks's first new collection in nearly ten years, pairs its long title poem with shorter poems on contemporary figures and events, among them Medgar Evers, Malcolm X, the Chicago Picasso, the Wall mural and the Blackstone Rangers.
literary_significance: A key poem of Brooks's late-1960s transformation and of the Black Arts era's attention to the black city.
bibliographical_notes: Published in In the Mecca (New York: Harper and Row, 1968), in three parts: I. As Seen by Disciplines; II. The Leaders; III. Gang Girls. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, vol. E (no page numbers).
thematic_analysis: The poem refuses the official view of the gang as a social disease and imagines its members from inside, as a self-made nation and as young people with longings of their own; it reflects Brooks's new commitment to the black community after 1967.
summary: The gang as seen by those who would discipline it; its leaders; and a 'Rangerette', one of the gang girls.
research_notes: The quotations are stated from the text. Brooks's writing workshop of 1967, which drew in young members of the gang, is general knowledge, not checked.

title: To the Diaspora
description: A poem by Gwendolyn Brooks in To Disembark (1981), published by Third World Press, subtitled 'you did not know you were Afrika': an address to black people of the diaspora on a journey towards Africa that turns out to be a journey into themselves.
plot_or_argument: When you set out for Afrika, the speaker tells the diaspora, you did not know you were going, because you did not know you were Afrika, that the black continent that had to be reached was you. The speaker could not have told you then that some sun would come, evoking the diamonds of you; you would not have believed it, and when told you smiled and thanked her but hardly believed. Here is some sun, the poem says, and now off into the places rough to reach: your work, that was done, to be done to be done to be done.
narrative_structure: Free-verse paragraphs addressed to 'you', moving from the journey to the speaker's prophecy and to the repeated, open-ended last line.
meter_and_prosody: Direct address, the spelling 'Afrika', repetition and incantation in the closing line.
historical_context: After 1967 Brooks left Harper and published with black presses such as Broadside Press and Third World Press; To Disembark gathers poems of this period.
literary_significance: A representative late poem of Brooks's Black Arts commitment, and the latest of her poems that Norton prints.
bibliographical_notes: Published in To Disembark (Chicago: Third World Press, 1981). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, vol. E (no page numbers).
thematic_analysis: Black identity and self-discovery: Africa is found within rather than abroad, and pride is the beginning of a labour that never ends.
summary: An address to 'you', who set out for Africa without knowing that the black continent to be reached was yourself; the speaker's earlier, disbelieved prophecy; a call to the hard work still to be done.
research_notes: The paraphrase is stated from the text. Brooks's move to black presses is general knowledge, not checked.

title: Our Bog Is Dood
description: A poem by Stevie Smith from Harold's Leap (1950): children lisp that 'Our Bog is dood', and the speaker's questions expose a faith held only because they wish it, ready to crucify the doubter.
plot_or_argument: 'Our Bog is dood,' the children lisp, but when the speaker asks them to explain they grow a little wild. They know their Bog is dood because they wish it so, they cry, and if she does not think it so she shall be crucified. Asked what 'dood' is, they answer that it is just what they think it is; they bow their heads: their Bog is theirs and they are wholly his. When they raise their heads they have forgotten her, and glare at one another in pride and misery, for they can never agree what their Bog is. It is sweet to leave them and to walk alone beside the encroaching sea, which will soon drown them all.
narrative_structure: Rhymed quatrains of ballad metre, moving from dialogue to the children's quarrel and the speaker's closing solitude.
meter_and_prosody: Nursery-rhyme simplicity and baby talk put to sharp theological satire; the liturgical echo of 'Our Bog is ours / And we are wholly his'.
historical_context: Written in the post-war years in which Smith moved between the Anglican faith of her childhood and the unbelief she later defended in 'The Necessity of Not Believing' (1958).
literary_significance: One of Smith's best-known poems on religion, often read as 'Our God is good' (or 'dead') in baby talk, and a Norton selection.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Harold's Leap (London: Jonathan Cape, 1950). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 586.
thematic_analysis: A satire on dogmatic belief as wish-fulfilment, with the sectarian hatred it breeds; the baby talk turns 'God is good' into nonsense and exposes faith held without understanding.
summary: A dialogue between the speaker and a group of children about their 'Bog', ending with the children quarrelling and the speaker walking alone by the sea.
research_notes: The paraphrase is stated from the text. A University of Minho dissertation dates the poem to 1950 and cites James Najarian (2003) on its echo of Anglican liturgy.

title: Not Waving but Drowning
description: Stevie Smith's most famous poem, published in 1957 in the collection of the same title and printed with one of her drawings: a dead man, whose movements in the sea were taken for waving, insists that he was drowning, and always had been.
plot_or_argument: Nobody heard him, the dead man, but still he lay moaning: he was much further out than they thought, and not waving but drowning. The onlookers say what people say: poor chap, he always loved larking, and now he is dead; it must have been too cold for him, his heart gave way. No, no, no, the dead man answers, still moaning, it was too cold always; he was much too far out all his life, and not waving but drowning. A remembered accident at sea becomes a figure for a whole life of misunderstood distress, in which the signals of despair were read as high spirits.
narrative_structure: Three quatrains in loose rhyme; the dead man's voice frames the bystanders' clichés in the middle stanza, and the refrain returns transformed from a single moment to 'all my life'.
meter_and_prosody: Simple, colloquial diction that Clive James saw as carefully crafted to seem ignorant of convention; the macabre comedy of a dead man still moaning; the incongruous drawing of a smiling girl.
historical_context: Smith was treated for depression and had contemplated suicide; she retired from Newnes after a breakdown in 1953. The poem appeared in Not Waving but Drowning (André Deutsch, 1957).
literary_significance: The most famous of Smith's poems and one of the best-known English poems of the century, its title a proverbial phrase for unnoticed despair.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Not Waving but Drowning (London: André Deutsch, 1957). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 587.
thematic_analysis: Isolation and misunderstanding: others mistake a cry for help for a cheerful wave, and the joking manner that hides suffering also prevents its being seen. Critics have read the drowning man as Smith herself, treated for depression, while noting that the poem's humour resists being read simply as a cry for help.
summary: The onlookers' comments on a drowned man who 'always loved larking', set against the dead man's own words: he was much further out than they thought, all his life, and not waving but drowning.
critical_context: Ingrid Hotz-Davies reads the drowning man as Smith but warns against reading the poem only as a cry for help; Laura Severin discusses the drawing's 'mysterious smile'; Janice Thaddeus sees an androgyny of speakers in Smith's work; Clive James wrote that her poems, if pills to cure melancholy, did not work for her, but worked like charms for everyone else.
research_notes: Critical views are as reported by Wikipedia (citing Sternlicht, Hotz-Davies, Severin, Thaddeus and James); none of those works was consulted directly.

title: Thoughts About the Person from Porlock
description: A poem by Stevie Smith that first appeared in her Selected Poems (1962): a comic revision of the story of the visitor who interrupted Coleridge's 'Kubla Khan', which turns into the speaker's longing to be interrupted herself.
plot_or_argument: Coleridge received the Person from Porlock and ever after called him a curse, but why did he hurry to let him in? The truth, the speaker suspects, is that he was already stuck with 'Kubla Khan', and the visitor took the blame. She imagines the Person's modest life at the bottom of the hill, with a cat named Flo, and then admits that she longs for him herself, to bring her thoughts to an end; she runs to the gate and is hungry to be interrupted for ever and ever. The poem ends with mock-cheerful advice to smile and submit to the purposes of One Above, who is experimenting with human characters.
narrative_structure: Stanzas of uneven length with irregular rhyme, moving from literary anecdote to confession and a sardonic close.
meter_and_prosody: Chatty, digressive and comic, with nonsense touches (the warlock grandmother, the cat named Flo) and a sudden darkening of tone.
historical_context: Selected Poems (Longmans, 1962) gathered Smith's earlier work with seventeen previously unpublished poems at the time her readings and broadcasts were winning new readers.
literary_significance: A favourite of anthologists and of writers on the 'Person from Porlock' legend, and a Norton selection.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Selected Poems (London: Longmans, 1962). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 588.
thematic_analysis: Creative block and the excuses of poets; the wish for thought, and life, to be interrupted, which carries Smith's familiar longing for death; an ironic view of providence.
summary: Coleridge and the Person from Porlock; the visitor's imagined life; the speaker's own wish for a Person from Porlock to bring her thoughts to an end; a closing reflection on smiling and submitting.
research_notes: The first publication in Selected Poems (1962) rests on Jeremy Noel-Tod's newsletter essay, seen as a search extract, and is corroborated by two poets' websites; the paraphrase is stated from the text.

title: Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night
description: Dylan Thomas's villanelle urging his father to 'rage, rage against the dying of the light', first published in the journal Botteghe Oscure in 1951 and collected in In Country Sleep and Collected Poems, 1934-1952 (both 1952). It is one of his best-known poems.
plot_or_argument: Old age should burn and rave at close of day, the speaker says: do not go gentle into that good night; rage, rage against the dying of the light. Wise men know at their end that dark is right, but because their words forked no lightning they do not go gently. Good men, seeing how bright their frail deeds might have danced, rage against the dying of the light. Wild men who caught and sang the sun in flight, and learn too late that they grieved it on its way, do not go gentle. Grave men near death, who see with blinding sight that blind eyes could blaze like meteors, rage too. In the last stanza the speaker turns to his father, 'there on the sad height', and asks him to curse and bless him now with his fierce tears, repeating both refrains.
narrative_structure: A villanelle: five tercets and a closing quatrain, nineteen lines on two rhymes, with two refrains ('Do not go gentle into that good night' and 'Rage, rage against the dying of the light') alternating and joined at the end.
meter_and_prosody: Incantatory iambic pentameter; puns ('good night', 'grave men') and paradoxes ('blinding sight', 'curse, bless'); intense, rhetorical repetition.
historical_context: Thomas's father, David John Thomas, a schoolmaster, was going blind and died just before Christmas 1952; Wikipedia reports that the poem was written in 1947 in Florence, though its dating and its connection with his father's illness are disputed. It was printed in Botteghe Oscure, the Rome review, in 1951.
literary_significance: One of the most famous villanelles in English and among the best-known poems of the century, often quoted and set to music (Stravinsky's In Memoriam Dylan Thomas sets the full text).
bibliographical_notes: First published in Botteghe Oscure (1951); collected in In Country Sleep, and Other Poems (New Directions, 1952) and Collected Poems, 1934-1952 (Dent, 1952). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 693.
thematic_analysis: Resistance to death and the refusal of resignation, set against the knowledge that death is right and necessary; the son's love for a dying father; the regret of lives unfulfilled. Seamus Heaney saw in the form a figure of the union of opposites, balancing natural grief and the recognition of necessity.
summary: The speaker's appeal to his father not to accept death quietly, supported by four kinds of men, wise, good, wild and grave, who each in their way rage against the end.
critical_context: Heaney called it 'obviously a threshold poem about death'; Jonathan Westphal reads the 'sad height' as a metaphorical plateau of loneliness before death, while Walford Davies hears King Lear on the heath and Gloucester at Dover cliff.
research_notes: Wikipedia states that Thomas wrote the poem in 1947 in Florence (citing Ferris) and flags as failed verification its claim that the poem was written for his dying father. The composition date is not recorded for that reason.

title: Colonization in Reverse
description: A poem by Louise Bennett, collected in Jamaica Labrish (1966), in which a Jamaican speaker tells Miss Mattie the 'joyful news' that Jamaicans are emigrating to England by the shipload and the planeload, colonising England in reverse.
plot_or_argument: 'Wat a joyful news, Miss Mattie,' the speaker begins, she feels as if her heart will burst: Jamaica people are colonising England in reverse. By the hundred and the thousand, from country and from town, by the shipload and the planeload, Jamaica is England bound. Everyone's future plan is to get a big-time job and settle in the mother land; some set up cheap-fare-to-England agencies to show their loyalty. Once they arrive, the speaker goes on, they find their different roles, and some prefer to draw the dole rather than work, since England is now paying them. What an island, what a people, she exclaims, who faced war and braved the worst; but she wonders how the English will stand being colonised in reverse.
narrative_structure: Ballad quatrains rhyming on the second and fourth lines, addressed throughout to Miss Mattie, a recurrent listener in Bennett's poems who creates the illusion of a dialogue.
literary_form: Poem (dramatic monologue in Jamaican Creole, ballad quatrains)
meter_and_prosody: Jamaican Creole in the rhythms of speech and of mento song; irony, hyperbole and puns; written for performance.
historical_context: Large-scale migration from Jamaica to Britain followed the Second World War, from the arrival of the Empire Windrush in 1948 until the Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962. Bennett, who had lived in England in the late 1940s, collected the poem in Jamaica Labrish (Sangster's, 1966), introduced by Rex Nettleford.
literary_significance: Bennett's best-known poem and a classic of Caribbean writing on the Windrush migration, widely anthologised, taught and performed.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in Jamaica Labrish (Kingston: Sangster's Book Stores, 1966), pp. 179-180. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 722.
thematic_analysis: The poem turns the history of empire upside down: the colonised now settle the 'mother country'. Its comedy mocks both the migrants' grand hopes and English fears of immigration, and asserts Jamaican language and wit as a match for the coloniser's.
summary: The speaker's account of the post-war migration of Jamaicans to Britain, their hopes of good jobs, their readiness to live on the dole, and her wonder at how England will stand being colonised in reverse.
critical_context: Eric Doumerc reads Bennett's poems as rooted in the mento tradition, with Miss Mattie as the average Jamaican woman and comic distance used to defuse hardship; postcolonial critics read the poem as subversive mimicry of colonial rhetoric.
research_notes: The earliest printing was not established; the subject (migration after 1948) places its writing within the period. The page numbers come from Doumerc and from an article in the Journal of Contemporary Issues in Education, both citing Jamaica Labrish. The paraphrase is stated from the text; the dates of the migration are general knowledge.

title: History of the Voice
alternative_titles: History of the Voice: The Development of Nation Language in Anglophone Caribbean Poetry
description: Kamau Brathwaite's History of the Voice: The Development of Nation Language in Anglophone Caribbean Poetry (London: New Beacon Books, 1984), a lecture-essay that named 'nation language', the English of the Caribbean's African-descended people, and argued that Caribbean poetry must break with the pentameter. Norton prints an excerpt under the title 'Nation Language'.
plot_or_argument: Brathwaite begins from the linguistic history of the Caribbean, where the imported languages of slaves and labourers were suppressed and given the status of inferiority, while the colonisers' languages became official. What English has given the Caribbean as a model for poetry is the pentameter, which carries an experience that is not the islands' own: 'The hurricane does not roar in pentameters.' The problem is how to find a rhythm close to the natural and environmental experience. His answer is nation language, which he distinguishes from 'dialect', a word carrying the pejorative overtones of caricature: an English that is not the standard, imported, educated English, but that of the submerged, surrealist experience and sensibility that has always been there and is now coming to the surface. Nation language is strongly influenced by African models; it is oral, so that its noise, rhythm and timbre are part of its meaning, and it is tied to the music of the region, from calypso to dub. He credits T. S. Eliot with introducing the notion of the speaking voice and the conversational tone, and traces the line of poets and performers, from Louise Bennett to the dub poets, who have made nation language a literary medium.
narrative_structure: A lecture expanded into an essay, moving from history to theory and to illustration, with many quoted and performed examples.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational and performative, close to the spoken lecture, with Brathwaite's own coinages and typographic emphasis.
historical_context: Brathwaite gave the lecture in 1979 (Wikipedia lists a History of the Voice of that year) and published the expanded text with New Beacon Books, the London publisher associated with John La Rose and the Caribbean Artists Movement, in 1984; it came out of the movement's debates of the late 1960s on Caribbean aesthetics.
literary_significance: The publication established Brathwaite as the authority on nation language, the term now commonly preferred to 'dialect' for the non-standard English of Caribbean and African diaspora writing; 'the hurricane does not roar in pentameters' is among the most quoted sentences of Caribbean criticism.
bibliographical_notes: History of the Voice: The Development of Nation Language in Anglophone Caribbean Poetry (London: New Beacon Books, 1984). Norton's excerpt, '[Nation Language]', is a selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 725.
thematic_analysis: Language as a site of colonial power and of resistance; the recovery of submerged African culture; the claim that Caribbean experience needs its own forms and rhythms; the unity of word, sound and music in an oral tradition.
summary: An account of the languages of the Caribbean and of the submergence of African languages under English; the tyranny of the pentameter; the definition of nation language; its oral and musical qualities; the poets, calypsonians and performers who have used it.
critical_context: Later critics apply its arguments to oral and performance poetry, disaster writing and social media, and set it beside Glissant's 'forced poetics'; some note its debt to Eliot's conversational tone, which Brathwaite himself acknowledged.
research_notes: Quotations come from articles citing the 1984 edition (pp. 7-16) seen as search extracts; the 1979 lecture is inferred from Wikipedia's list of works, and its venue was not established. The discussion of Louise Bennett and New Beacon's association with La Rose are general knowledge.

title: Calypso
description: A poem from Kamau Brathwaite's Rights of Passage (1967), the first book of The Arrivants trilogy: a history of the Caribbean islands from their creation to the tourist present, told in the rhythms of calypso.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the islands' creation: a stone skids, arcs and blooms into islands, Cuba and San Domingo, Jamaica and Puerto Rico, Grenada, Guadeloupe, Bonaire. The islands then roar into green plantations ruled by silver sugar cane, sweat and profit, and history becomes the story of slavery and the plantation. In the present the steel drums beat and the rum flows in a carnival that no one can stop, while the tourist trade keeps the islanders in service.
narrative_structure: Several sections in different rhythms, from the incantatory list of island names to calypso and dance measures, forming one movement of Rights of Passage.
literary_form: Poem (section of the sequence Rights of Passage)
meter_and_prosody: Short, percussive lines; place-names as music; calypso rhythm and Caribbean speech; irony beneath celebration.
historical_context: Rights of Passage (1967) follows the African diaspora from Africa to the Caribbean and the cities of the West; with Masks (1968) and Islands (1969) it formed The Arrivants (1973), generally considered Brathwaite's best work.
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised parts of The Arrivants and an early demonstration of Brathwaite's use of Caribbean musical forms.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Rights of Passage (London: Oxford University Press, 1967); reprinted in The Arrivants: A New World Trilogy (1973). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 730.
thematic_analysis: The bright surface of Caribbean pleasure set against its history of slavery and its present of dependence; the music of calypso used to tell an unhappy story.
summary: The islands imagined as a stone skipped across the sea; their transformation into sugar plantations; the carnival and steel band of the present; the servility of the tourist economy.
research_notes: The paraphrase and the description of Rights of Passage are stated from general knowledge of the text, not from a consulted source, and the publisher of Rights of Passage is general knowledge; the dates of the trilogy come from Wikipedia.

title: Letter SycoraX
description: A poem by Kamau Brathwaite in Middle Passages (1992): Caliban writes to his mother Sycorax on the computer, in nation language and in the computer fonts, sizes and layouts that Brathwaite called 'Sycorax video style'. It revises 'X/Self xth letter from the thirteenth provinces' from X/Self (1987).
plot_or_argument: Caliban, the colonised slave of The Tempest, writes a letter to his mother Sycorax, the poem's 'X', telling her about the computer he is learning to write on and about the language he is making of the master's English. The letter mixes complaint, comedy and visionary excitement; its broken words, spellings and changing fonts and sizes make the page itself part of the meaning, and the letter X recurs as a visual sign of Sycorax and of the unnamed self.
narrative_structure: A long verse letter with salutation and sign-off, its layout varied by font, size and alignment.
literary_form: Poem (verse letter in nation language and 'Sycorax video style')
meter_and_prosody: Nation language, puns and neologisms, and typographic experiment that slows and complicates reading.
historical_context: Brathwaite developed the Sycorax video style after the 'time of salt' of 1986-1990, the death of his wife, the loss of his archive to Hurricane Gilbert and a near-fatal attack; Middle Passages printed the poem while, its publishers noted, the style was still being developed.
literary_significance: A key text of Brathwaite's late experimental poetics and of Caribbean rewritings of The Tempest.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Middle Passages (Newcastle upon Tyne: Bloodaxe, 1992; New York: New Directions, 1993), a revision of 'X/Self xth letter from the thirteenth provinces' in X/Self (1987). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1103.
thematic_analysis: The colonised writer's struggle with Prospero's language and technology, turned into a new medium of expression; the recovery of the suppressed mother; revision as survival after catastrophe.
summary: A letter from Caliban to his mother, the witch Sycorax of The Tempest, about writing on the computer and about language, power and memory, set out in shifting typefaces.
research_notes: The publication history comes from a study of the versions of the X/Self letter (seen as a search extract), which counts four printings, each revised. The publishers of Middle Passages are general knowledge. The paraphrase is general, since the text was not consulted.

title: Decolonising the Mind
alternative_titles: Decolonising the Mind: The Politics of Language in African Literature
description: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's Decolonising the Mind: The Politics of Language in African Literature (London: James Currey, 1986), four essays arguing that African writers should write in African languages; it is his 'farewell to English' and one of the most cited texts of postcolonial studies. Norton prints part of the first essay, 'The Language of African Literature'.
plot_or_argument: Ngũgĩ describes the book as a summary of issues in which he had been passionately involved for twenty years of fiction, theatre, criticism and teaching. The first essay argues that language carries culture and that the imposition of European languages on African children, through schools that punished them for speaking their mother tongues, separated them from their own history and community and colonised the mind; he recalls his own schooling in Gikuyu and then in English. Writing in English or French, however brilliant, builds a literature for an elite and for foreign readers. The second essay tells the story of the Kamiriithu theatre and of the play Ngaahika Ndeenda, performed in Gikuyu by villagers until the government closed it; the third describes the writing of his first Gikuyu novel, Caitaani Mũtharaba-inĩ, in prison; the fourth calls for African literature, languages and peoples to be placed at the centre of education. He closes by bidding farewell to English as the vehicle of any of his writing.
narrative_structure: Four essays, several of them first given as lectures, with an introduction and a statement of farewell.
literary_form: Essays (four lectures on language and literature)
meter_and_prosody: Direct, polemical and autobiographical, combining memoir with Marxist and anti-imperialist analysis.
historical_context: After the closure of Ngaahika Ndeenda in 1977 Ngũgĩ was imprisoned without trial and, on his release, went into exile; he had already turned to Gikuyu for his fiction. The book entered the 'language debate' of postcolonial studies, opposed by writers such as Achebe and Rushdie who defended the use of English.
literary_significance: One of Ngũgĩ's best-known and most cited works, which made him the pre-eminent voice in the debate on African languages; it is a standard text of postcolonial theory courses.
bibliographical_notes: Decolonising the Mind: The Politics of Language in African Literature (London: James Currey; Nairobi: Heinemann Kenya, 1986), 114 pages. Norton's excerpt, from 'The Language of African Literature', is a selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 732.
thematic_analysis: Language as both means of communication and carrier of culture; colonial education as cultural domination; neocolonialism; the writer's choice of medium, audience and purpose; the dignity of African languages.
summary: Four essays, 'The Language of African Literature', 'The Language of African Theatre', 'The Language of African Fiction' and 'The Quest for Relevance', mixing autobiography, history, theory and pedagogy.
critical_context: Oliver Lovesey calls it the book that cemented his place in the language debate; critics weigh its call for African languages against the practical case for English as a means of international communication and of subversive appropriation.
research_notes: The Heinemann Kenya imprint, the account of his schooling and the content of the third and fourth essays are general knowledge; the essays' titles, the farewell to English and the dedication come from Wikipedia. The excerpt's title is the CSV's 'From The Language of African Literature'.
